question_text: A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. He is a 35-pack-year smoker. His blood pressure is 155/95 mm Hg. His BMI is 37 kg/m2. Oropharyngeal examination shows a small orifice and an enlarged tongue and uvula. The soft palate is low-lying. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A 65-year-old man presents to the physician for the evaluation of increasing dyspnea and swelling of the lower extremities over the past year. He has no cough. He also complains of frequent awakenings at night and excessive daytime sleepiness. He has no history of a serious illness. He takes no medications other than zolpidem before sleep. The examination of the nasal cavity shows no septal deviation or polyps. Symmetric pitting edema is seen below the knee, bilaterally. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Echocardiography shows a mildly dilated right ventricle and an elevated systolic pulmonary artery pressure with no abnormalities of the left heart. A ventilation-perfusion scan shows no abnormalities. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
opb. Heart failure with a preserved ejection fraction
opc. Idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension
opd. Obstructive sleep apnea
ope. Pulmonary thromboembolism

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms are most consistent with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The reasoning chains for OSA align with medical consensus: OSA leads to intermittent hypoxia, causing pulmonary vasoconstriction and elevated pulmonary artery pressure, which can result in right ventricular dilation, dyspnea, and lower extremity edema. The patient's obesity, enlarged tongue, and uvula contribute to airway obstruction during sleep, further supporting OSA. The evidence paths confirm that hypoxia can cause pulmonary hypertension and that airway obstruction can lead to hypoxia. The patient's excessive daytime sleepiness and frequent awakenings at night are classic symptoms of OSA. Other options, such as idiopathic pulmonary artery hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, and pulmonary thromboembolism, are less likely due to the absence of specific supporting findings, such as clear lungs on auscultation, no left heart abnormalities, and a normal ventilation-perfusion scan. Therefore, obstructive sleep apnea is the most likely cause of the patient's symptoms.
